explanations.answer: That they will not enter into temptation
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jesus tells them, “Pray that you will not enter into temptation.” No long speech and no fine print, just one clear thing to pray. He says it again in verse 46.

explanations.answer: That the crowds will leave them alone
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say a word about crowds in this instruction. A crowd does show up a few verses later, so I see why it came to mind. But what He asks them to pray is “…that you will not enter into temptation.” Keep that one in your pocket, friend.

explanations.answer: That the city will welcome their message
explanations.explanation: Nothing about the city or a message comes up here, baker. Jesus keeps it close to home and tells them, “Pray that you will not enter into temptation.” It's short and simple. That's what He asks them to pray, and He repeats it in verse 46.

Close, friend, but it flips right at the end. Jesus does ask for the cup to be taken, and then He says, “Yet not My will, but Yours be done.” So He doesn't pray for His own will. He hands it over to the Father's.

Right, baker. The text says Jesus prays, “Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me. Yet not My will, but Yours be done.” So after the ask, He doesn't push for His own will. He prays for the Father's will to be done.
Yes, baker. Verse 43 says an angel from heaven appeared to Him and strengthened Him. He's out there praying alone, and heaven sends help. I think that's a quiet kind of kindness.

Elijah does appear and speak with Jesus in another scene (Luke 9:30-31). But he's not in this one. Here the text says an angel from heaven appeared to Him and strengthened Him. Different scene, friend.
Moses does appear and speak with Jesus in a different moment (Luke 9:30-31). Not here, though, baker. In this passage, “…an angel from heaven appeared to Him and strengthened Him.” That's the one.

Yes, baker. The text says that in His anguish, He prayed more earnestly, “…and His sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground.” I think this one hurts to read. It tells us how heavy this night was for Him.

The text says it is true, friend. In His anguish, Jesus prayed more earnestly, “…and His sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground.” I think this is one of the heaviest lines in the whole passage. So we slow down and let it sit.
That's right, baker. Verse 45 says Jesus found them asleep, exhausted from sorrow. Then He asks, “Why are you sleeping?” That question comes in verse 46.
Praying is a fair guess, friend. But when Jesus returned, He found them asleep. Then He asks, “Why are you sleeping?” They weren't praying.
Nice try, baker, but nobody's on lookout duty here. When Jesus gets back from praying, He finds the disciples asleep. Then He tells them to get up and pray.
Yes, friend. The text says they were “…exhausted from sorrow.” This was no ordinary nap. It was a heavy night for them.
Travel is a fair guess, baker, since they did walk out to the Mount of Olives. But the text gives a different reason. It says they were “…exhausted from sorrow.”
Picture a long shift followed by a bed, baker. I get why that came to mind, but the text doesn't say that. It says they were “…exhausted from sorrow.” Sorrow wears a person out in its own way.

Yes, baker. Verse 47 says Judas “…approached Jesus to kiss Him.” It's a greeting people know well, and it's what he walks up to do in front of the whole crowd. Then Jesus says something about it, and we get to that next.
The text doesn't say Judas bows. It says he approached Jesus to kiss Him. That's what he came to do, friend, right in front of the crowd.
Feet come to mind, since Jesus washes His disciples' feet in John 13:5. But that isn't what Judas approaches Him to do here, baker. Verse 47 says he approached Jesus to kiss Him.

explanations.answer: The servant of the high priest
explanations.explanation: That's him, baker. Verse 50 says one of them struck the servant of the high priest. The high priest was the top priest. The text doesn't name the swordsman or the servant here.
Judas is the one who walked up to Jesus, so he'd be the natural guess. But verse 50 says the man struck the servant of the high priest, friend. That's who took the hit.

A centurion was an officer in the Roman army, but this passage never mentions one. The text says the one who got struck was the servant of the high priest. Keep your eyes on who's actually in the scene, baker.
Yes, friend. Verse 50 says the sword cut off the servant's right ear. The text is exact about which side. That's the ear Jesus touches in verse 51.
That's it, baker. The sword cut off the servant's ear. That's why Jesus touches an ear in verse 51.
Not the left one, friend. Verse 50 says it was his right ear. This is a heavy moment, so it's worth reading slowly.
Hands are a fair guess for a sword swing. But the text says the sword cut off the servant's right ear. And that's the very spot Jesus touches next.
Not an arm, friend. Verse 50 says the sword cut off his right ear. And in verse 51, Jesus touches the man's ear and heals him.
That's right, baker. Verse 51 says Jesus “…touched the man’s ear and healed him.” Just before that, He says, “No more of this!” In the middle of the arrest, He heals the servant.
The text says it's true, friend. After saying, “No more of this!” Jesus touched the man's ear and healed him. The servant is the one who was hurt in this scene, and Jesus is the One who heals him.
Yes, baker. Jesus asks, “Have you come out with swords and clubs as you would against an outlaw?” It's a pointed question. He's not hiding and He's not fighting, and He lets them see the picture.

Swords can make you think soldier, friend, and I get it. But Jesus is speaking to the chief priests, temple officers, and elders, and His question is, “Have you come out with swords and clubs as you would against an outlaw?” Outlaw is the word He picks.
I know that's a lot of swords and clubs, baker. But Jesus doesn't talk about animals. His question is, “Have you come out with swords and clubs as you would against an outlaw?”
It's the reverse, baker. Jesus says, “Every day I was with you in the temple courts, and you did not lay a hand on Me.” Every day, and no hand laid on Him. That's what He tells them.

Right, friend. Jesus says, “Every day I was with you in the temple courts, and you did not lay a hand on Me.” So all those days in the temple, no hands laid on Him. He says it to the chief priests, temple officers, and elders who had come for Him.
Yes, baker. Jesus says, “But this hour belongs to you and to the power of darkness.” It's a heavy line, and He says it plainly. I'd read it slowly.
Rome is a fair guess, baker, but Jesus doesn't name it in what He says. He says, “But this hour belongs to you and to the power of darkness.” That last part is what He names.

I can see why that one tempts you, friend, but Jesus doesn't say it. He says it to the chief priests, temple officers, and elders who had come for Him: “But this hour belongs to you and to the power of darkness.” It's a heavy line, so I'd read it slowly.
